summary:
ARES-EVA is a web-based tactical planner for Mars extravehicular activities (EVAs), helping the first human explorers decide where to walk, what to study, and when to turn back. We built an interactive application set in Mount Sharp (Gale Crater) that layers NASA-inspired datasets into a single map: HiRISE optical imagery, DEM-style slope analysis, CRISM mineralogy (sulfates and clays), THEMIS thermal inertia, and 5 m contour lines. As a prototype, the terrain is procedurally generated and simulated to mirror the region’s geology, and it is designed to be connected to real mission datasets.

It addresses the challenge through autonomous navigation using a safety-weighted A* algorithm that avoids slopes above 18° and dust traps, and re-plans the route whenever a new science target is selected. It also provides suit telemetry, a first-person AR-HUD view, and a solar storm simulation that triggers a rapid escape route to shelter.

This matters because crewed missions will demand fast decisions from scattered information. Combining science, safety, and logistics in one hyperlocal tool reduces risk and maximizes the scientific return of every EVA.
details:
What it does and how it works

ARES-EVA is a web-based tactical planner for the first human extravehicular activities (EVAs) on Mars. It centers on a 2.5 × 2.5 km area of Mount Sharp (Gale Crater), divided into a grid of 100 × 100 cells of 25 m each. Users see a multilayer map with HiRISE-style optical shading, a slope and risk layer (green below 12°, amber 12°–18°, red above 18°), CRISM-style mineral signatures (sulfates and clays), THEMIS-style thermal inertia (firm rock vs. dust traps) and 5 m contour lines. Each layer can be toggled and its opacity adjusted.

Clicking any point on the map sets a new science target. A safety-weighted A* algorithm then computes a route that avoids steep slopes and dust traps, for both the astronaut pair and the MULE cargo rover. During the simulated traverse, the app shows suit telemetry (oxygen, PLSS battery, radiation dose, metabolic rate), plus a first-person AR-HUD view of the Martian horizon. A solar storm simulation raises a radiation alert and traces a rapid escape route to a shielded refuge.

Benefits

ARES-EVA puts science, safety and logistics in one tool. It reduces the risk of unsafe routes, speeds up decisions under pressure and helps crews prioritize the most valuable geological targets on each outing.

Intended impact

We want to support safer, more productive surface operations for future crewed Mars missions. It could also serve as a training and mission-planning prototype for EVA teams.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no backend)
  • HTML5 Canvas 2D for the tactical map and the first-person view
  • Tailwind CSS, Google Fonts (Inter, JetBrains Mono) and Font Awesome for the interface
  • A custom A* pathfinding implementation and a deterministic procedural terrain generator
  • Data inspired by NASA instruments (MRO HiRISE, CRISM, THEMIS) and USGS topography

Creativity

Instead of a static map viewer, we built a mission-control experience: layered science data, autonomous routing, a live suit telemetry panel and an emergency contingency mode that reacts in real time. The interface follows a JPL-style HUD aesthetic to feel like a real operations console.

Factors we considered

  • Astronaut safety: slope limits, loose dust and radiation exposure
  • Consumables: oxygen and battery use over the route
  • Scientific value: routing toward mineral-rich boxwork ridges
  • Speed and simplicity: a single-file web app that runs in any browser
  • Scalability: the prototype uses simulated terrain based on Mount Sharp, built so real NASA datasets can be connected later
